[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Omadacycline, the closest supplied tetracycline-class analog to the query fluorocycline, has measured absolute oral bioavailability of 34.5% in healthy adults after a 300 mg fasted standard tablet, 31.2% in CF patients, and 31% in monkeys, all above the 20% threshold.

Tetracycline has human oral bioavailability reported as 75%, >70%, and 80–90%, and L3 oral exposure records show substantial absorption (500 mg tetracycline alone: geometric mean Cmax 4.57 µg/mL and AUC0-∞ 67.4 µg·h/mL in healthy volunteers), supporting that the tetracycline core can achieve F≥20% in humans.
L5 doxycycline Caco-2 records show A-B Papp of 3.4 ± 0.23 ×10^-6 cm/s and an efflux ratio of 1.2, indicating that the tetracycline class can exhibit good permeability and minimal P-gp efflux.

L5 tetracycline P-gp substrate and mucin-barrier records are class-level mechanistic concerns, but tetracycline itself has high human oral bioavailability; they are not affirmative evidence that the query fluorocycline has F<20%.

No direct eravacycline-specific absolute oral bioavailability, permeability, or efflux record is supplied; the high prediction rests on class-level transfer and means F≥20% is better supported, not that a specific F value or formulation is established.

evidence_gaps: No direct eravacycline-specific absolute oral bioavailability, permeability, efflux, or intestinal-metabolism record is present in the supplied cards; the decision relies on transfer from omadacycline and tetracycline.

The target species is not explicitly specified; omadacycline lacks oral bioavailability in rodents (C108) and tetracycline rat in situ absorption is low (C220), so a rodent-based endpoint would substantially weaken the high prediction.
Formulation and prandial conditions for the query are unspecified; omadacycline F ranges from 0.5% for a slow-dissolution tablet to 34.5% for a standard fasted tablet (C49, C18).
Potential eravacycline-specific P-gp efflux and intestinal metabolism are not directly measured; L5 tetracycline P-gp/mucin records are class-level only.
Most L5 records are for unrelated molecules (fluoroquinolones, anthracyclines, nintedanib, danoprevir, etc.) and were not used as evidence for the query.
content.decision_summary: Predicted high (F≥20%) because the query is a fluorocycline tetracycline and the closest supplied empirical contexts—omadacycline (34.5% human, 31.2% CF, 31% monkey) and tetracycline (75% human)—show oral bioavailability above threshold; L3 oral exposure records for tetracycline (Cmax 4.57 µg/mL, AUC0-∞ 67.4 µg·h/mL at 500 mg) reinforce that the tetracycline class is orally absorbed; L5 adds mixed class-level gut-wall evidence (tetracycline P-gp/mucin barriers vs doxycycline good permeability and low efflux) that does not overturn the human class-level evidence; the low physicochemical prior is not affirmative evidence of F<20% and no new contradictory eravacycline-specific evidence was supplied.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L5 adds gut-wall efflux and intestinal-metabolism experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for presystemic loss, with direction and experimental context preserved; mechanism alone is not a direct oral-bioavailability result.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
